annotations.text:
Photo moved into the header band, two ways. Each artboard has a 'bleed' toggle.

OFF = B: the photograph sits sharp on the leading edge at its true size, a painted gradient carrying the rest. Night is an exact 1:1 pixel crop.

ON = A: the photograph fills the whole header, upscaled 1.9x (day) or 3.1x (night), blurred to hide it.

Turn A on and look at what is left of the photograph.

The photographic direction in two modes, using your own photographs.

The switch is driven by the clock, not a preference — the site turns dark at real shkia and light again at netz, the same way the Hebrew date rolls at sunset. The small sun/moon button beside the language switch lets you override it.

No photograph is stretched: every one renders below its native size. The night frame is portrait, so it gets a tall header on mobile and a tall narrow panel on desktop rather than being cropped into a letterbox.

Three directions, each now at phone size (top row) and full desktop width (below).

Built from photographs of the city rather than from architectural theory. Same content everywhere — same shuls, same times, same honest-unknown row — so this is a comparison of visual language.

Flip the Sunset toggle on any artboard.

What the extra width earned, per direction:

Photographic — the image now does two jobs at two scales: a scrimmed panoramic wash behind the masthead, and a crisp unscaled panel where the map placeholder used to be.

Night City — the gradient has room to actually gradate, plus a flat skyline silhouette and a night map with glowing pins.

Day Sea — a real horizon line, and the hero card overlaps the band edge with one curved corner: a balcony breaking a flat facade.

The photograph is real — Tel Aviv at blue hour by Martin Furtschegger, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons. Self-hosted, resized to 39KB, credited in the artboard as the licence requires.

Worth weighing: one photograph cannot represent 484 synagogues. Shipping this means either per-shul photography or a rotating set of city shots.
Kept for the record. All five were rejected as not looking like Tel Aviv — the palette is a desaturated version of the real thing.

Photographic with the map restored. The photograph moves entirely to the header band; the map returns to its own slot.

The designer deliberately kept the map as a drawn schematic rather than satellite imagery — its argument being that two photographs would leave the page with no functional layer at all, which is the opposite of what you asked for.
